svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. The Firefox hardening ladder, and the rungs most people skip past
svg.desc: Four tiers of Firefox configuration in increasing order. Tier one is the settings interface only, which brings Enhanced Tracking Protection strict and with it Total Cookie Protection. Tier two adds a content blocker and containers. Tier three turns on the light targeted fingerprinting protection. Tier four is the Tor-derived resist fingerprinting mode or a community preference file, which is global and breaks pages. A panel on the right lists preferences that older guides recommend and the reason each one should now be skipped.
svg.text: Figure 3: Climb the Ladder in Order, and Stop When It Is Enough
Most published guides start at tier 4. Tiers 1 and 2 carry most of the benefit and almost none of the breakage.
The settings interface, and nothing else

g.text: Enhanced Tracking Protection set to Strict. Telemetry and studies off. HTTPS-Only on.
Encrypted name resolution on. Permissions set to block by default.
What this buys: Strict brings Total Cookie Protection, which isolates storage per site.
A single well-maintained content blocker. Multi-Account Containers for separation
between your identities inside one browser.
What this buys: the unlinkability from Figure 1, question 3, at very low cost.
The lighter fingerprinting protection inside Enhanced Tracking Protection. This is what
Mozilla recommends for most people.
What this buys: real reduction, and it can be relaxed for one site without turning it all off.

svg.text: Resist Fingerprinting, or a community preference file

g.text: The Tor-derived uniformity mode. It forces one time zone, rounds the window with letterbox
bars, limits fonts, and prompts before a page can read canvas pixels. It does not add noise.
The catch: it is global. On or off, every tab, with no per-site relief. Pages will break.
Reach for this only when Figure 1 question 2 said yes, and then ask why you are not using Tor Browser.

svg.text: Preferences older guides tell you to set
Check each one before you copy it

g.text: privacy.firstparty.isolate
Superseded. Total Cookie Protection already does
this, is on with Strict, and breaks far less. Setting
both is redundant and causes problems.
dom.battery.enabled
Pointless in Firefox. The battery interface was
removed from Firefox years ago. It is Chrome
that still exposes it.
webgl.disabled
Heavy-handed. It breaks maps and charts, and
the absence of graphics support is itself an
unusual signal. Tier 3 or 4 already limits it.
network.http.referer.XOriginPolicy
Mostly redundant now. The browser default
already sends only the origin across sites.
Tightening it further mainly breaks sign-in flows.
media.peerconnection.enabled = false
Blunt. It disables video calling outright. The
local address leak this was written for is largely
closed already, as Lesson 2.1 covered.
The pattern behind all five
Each was good advice once. Each was copied
forward past the change that retired it.

svg.text: A preference name in a guide is not advice. It is advice with an expiry date that nobody printed on it.
Before you set one, find out what it does now, and what the browser already does without it.
